prompt: In the test pyramid, which characteristic generally increases as you move from unit tests up to end-to-end tests?
choices: Realism and confidence that the whole system works together as deployed
Speed of execution
Ease of pinpointing exactly which line of code failed
How many of them you should write relative to unit tests

prompt: What is the main practical cost of the 'ice cream cone' anti-pattern (few unit tests, heavy reliance on UI-driven e2e tests)?
choices: Slow, brittle suites that give feedback late and are expensive to debug and maintain
Too much test coverage on business logic
Contract tests become unnecessary once you have enough e2e tests
Unit tests start passing even when the code is broken

prompt: When you write `await expect(locator).toHaveText('3')` in Playwright, what happens before the assertion is reported as failed?
choices: Playwright retries the assertion against the live DOM for a timeout window until it passes or the window expires
It checks once immediately and fails right away if the text doesn't match yet
It waits for exactly one requestAnimationFrame and checks once
It restarts the whole test from the beginning

prompt: Why might a team write an API-level e2e test with Playwright's `request` fixture instead of driving the same flow through a full browser page?
choices: It exercises the real backend with much less overhead than rendering a browser, at the cost of not verifying the UI itself
It gives identical confidence to a browser test but runs slower
It removes the need for any unit tests in the codebase
Playwright requires an API test to pass before any browser test can run

prompt: What does a consumer-driven contract test (e.g. with Pact) actually verify?
choices: That the provider's real response for the exact interactions the consumer recorded still matches what the consumer expects
That the provider's entire API surface is free of bugs
That the two services behave correctly together under production load
That the consumer's own business logic is correct

prompt: order-service's Pact contract with inventory-service passes on both sides in CI, but production breaks after inventory-service ships a change. What's the most likely explanation?
choices: order-service started relying on a call or field that was never recorded in any pact interaction, so it fell outside what verification checked
Pact tests are inherently unreliable and shouldn't be trusted in CI
The provider verification must have run against the wrong port
Contract tests always catch this kind of break when both sides are green

prompt: A test that clicks 'Add to cart' three times intermittently ends with the wrong badge count in CI, because the three add-to-cart requests can return in a different order than they were sent. What is the actual bug?
choices: The client blindly applies whichever server response arrives last in wall-clock time, instead of applying only the response for the most recently sent request
The test doesn't wait long enough before making its assertion
The Playwright locator for the button isn't using auto-wait
The server is returning the wrong HTTP status code

prompt: Why is inserting an arbitrary `waitForTimeout(5000)` a bad fix for a flaky test caused by an out-of-order async response race?
choices: It only lowers the odds of hitting the race without fixing the defect, so the same bug can still surface under real production timing or load
Playwright test files don't support waitForTimeout at all
It makes the test suite finish noticeably faster
It permanently fixes the race by guaranteeing correct response ordering
